ml-w1d1: A model is a function with knobs. Supervised learns from answers, unsupervised finds structure without them, semi-supervised mixes a few answers with lots of unlabeled data, and reinforcement learns from rewards.
ml-w1d2: A dataset is a table: rows are examples (points in feature space), columns are features, and the label is the answer column. PyTorch stores it as a tensor of shape (n, d).
ml-w1d3: kNN labels a point by a vote of its kkk nearest training points. Small kkk gives jagged, noise-sensitive boundaries; large kkk gives smooth ones that can miss detail.
ml-w1d4: Judge a model only on data it never saw: train on one part, choose the knobs on a validation set or by cross-validation, and open the test set once, at the very end.
ml-w1d5: The confusion matrix shows every kind of mistake. Precision, recall, F1 and balanced accuracy each tell part of the story, and on rare classes they tell the truth when accuracy lies.
ml-w2d1: Linear regression picks the slope and intercept that make the mean squared error as small as possible; the least-squares line has an exact formula, and outliers pull on it hard.
ml-w2d2: Gradient descent repeats one move: compute the slope of the loss and step against it, by an amount set by the learning rate. Too small is slow, too large diverges.
ml-w2d3: PyTorch records how tensors are computed, so loss.backward() finds every gradient for you; training is always the same loop: zero the gradients, predict, compute the loss, backward, step.
ml-w2d4: Polynomial features let a linear model bend. Too little bending underfits (high bias), too much overfits (high variance), and validation error finds the sweet spot, which moves toward more flexibility as data grows.
ml-w2d5: Regularization keeps a flexible model calm by penalizing big weights: ridge (L2) shrinks them, lasso (L1) sets many to zero. Cross-validation decides how strong the penalty should be.
ml-w3d1: Logistic regression scores points with a line, squashes the score into a probability with the sigmoid, and learns by minimizing cross-entropy, which punishes confident mistakes.
ml-w3d2: Cross-entropy is the surprise −log⁡p-\log p−logp at the true class, and its gradient p−yp - yp−y keeps pushing on confident mistakes; softmax turns KKK scores into KKK probabilities, so the same loss trains classifiers with any number of classes.
ml-w3d3: On imbalanced data a model ignores the rare class because that's cheapest for the average loss; class weights, resampling or a lower threshold make it look, at the price of more false alarms, so judge it with recall, precision and the precision–recall curve.
ml-w3d4: A decision tree asks the one-feature question that leaves the purest groups, again and again, carving the plane into boxes; it's easy to read, but grown too deep it memorizes the noise.
ml-w3d5: Classifiers output scores that softmax turns into probabilities and cross-entropy trains; rare classes need weights, resampling or a new threshold; trees ask yes/no questions, and forests of them vote away their overfitting.
ml-w4d1: A feature map lifts data into a space where a linear model is enough; seen back in the original space, the straight boundary becomes curved.
ml-w4d2: An SVM finds the widest street between two classes; only the support vectors on its edges matter, CCC trades width for training mistakes, and underneath it's a linear model with hinge loss and a ridge penalty.
ml-w4d3: An SVM only needs similarities k(x,x′)=φ(x)⋅φ(x′)k(x, x') = \varphi(x)\cdot\varphi(x')k(x,x′)=φ(x)⋅φ(x′), so a kernel can replace a feature map we never compute; the RBF kernel uses infinitely many hidden features, with γ\gammaγ setting how local "similar" is.
ml-w4d4: The kernel matrix holds the similarity of every pair of points; a good one shows bright same-class blocks, too wide is all ones, too narrow is the identity, and SVC(kernel="precomputed") accepts any valid matrix you can compute.
ml-w4d5: Feature maps lift data, SVMs find the widest street, the kernel trick swaps features for similarities, the kernel matrix is all the SVM ever sees, and any valid similarity, quantum ones included, can join a fair benchmark.
ml-w5d1: A neuron weighs its inputs, adds a bias and applies an activation, drawing one straight boundary; the perceptron rule learns any problem a line can separate, but XOR needs more than one neuron.
ml-w5d2: A neural network stacks layers of weighted sums with nonlinear activations in between; the nonlinearity lets the boundary bend, and the network trains with the same loop as before.
ml-w5d3: Backpropagation computes the network forward, then sends the gradient of the loss backward with the chain rule, so one backward pass yields the gradient of every weight; autograd does exactly this inside loss.backward().
ml-w5d4: Real training steps with cheap, noisy mini-batch gradients, uses momentum or Adam to move sensibly through narrow valleys, and watches the validation loss so it can stop, and keep the best weights, before the network memorizes its training data.
ml-w5d5: A neural network stacks layers of weighted sums and nonlinear bends, learns all its weights at once with backpropagation, and trains well with mini-batches, Adam and early stopping; on clean digits it reaches 97%, and new kinds of data remind us that every model depends on what it was trained on.
ml-w6d1: k-means alternates "join the nearest center" and "move the center to the mean" until nothing changes; k-means++ starts and restarts avoid bad local minima, the elbow and the silhouette suggest kkk, and its straight borders suit round groups only.
ml-w6d2: A Gaussian mixture models the data as weighted bell-shaped blobs with their own shapes; EM alternates soft memberships (E) and re-fitting (M), raising the log-likelihood each round, and BIC chooses how many blobs to keep.
ml-w6d3: PCA finds the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, the directions of largest variance; keeping the top kkk gives the best straight-line compression, the explained-variance curve tells how many to keep, and features must be standardized first.
ml-w6d4: An autoencoder learns to copy its input through a narrow code: nonlinear layers let it compress better than PCA, its code space can be explored and decoded, its reconstruction error flags the unusual, and training noisy-in, clean-out makes it a denoiser.
ml-w6d5: Semi-supervised learning lets a few labels spread through the structure of many unlabeled points; graph methods follow the data's shape, while self-training must watch out for confirmation bias.
ml-w7d1: In reinforcement learning an agent acts, gets rewards and new states; an MDP lists the states, actions, transition probabilities, rewards and discount; the return discounts future rewards by γ\gammaγ; and a policy's value is its average return.
ml-w7d2: Reinforcement learning learns from rewards alone: estimate each action's value from experience, and balance exploring (to learn) with exploiting (to earn), for example with ε-greedy.
ml-w7d3: A state's value is its expected return; the Bellman equation says value now = reward + discounted value next, maximized over actions; value iteration applies it in sweeps until it settles, and the greedy policy on V∗V^*V∗ is optimal.
ml-w7d4: Q-learning estimates how good each action is in each state, nudging every guess towards "reward now plus the discounted value of where I land", so value flows backwards from the goal until the arrows point the way.
ml-w7d5: Reinforcement learning maximizes return in an MDP: bandits trade exploring against exploiting, value iteration plans with the Bellman equation, Q-learning learns the same values from experience, and policy gradients train a neural-network policy directly towards the moves that paid off.
qc-w1d1: A qubit is a pair of amplitudes (α,β)(\alpha, \beta)(α,β). Square them to get the probabilities of 0 and 1, which must add up to 1. One measurement gives one random bit; many shots reveal the probabilities.
qc-w1d2: Amplitudes are complex arrows. Their lengths set the 0/1 odds, a global phase means nothing, and the relative phase is real: it shows up when states are compared, P=∣⟨ϕ∣ψ⟩∣2P = |\langle\phi|\psi\rangle|^2P=∣⟨ϕ∣ψ⟩∣2.
qc-w1d3: A measurement gives one random bit and collapses the qubit. Probabilities come from many shots on fresh copies, and the estimate's error shrinks like 1/N1/\sqrt{N}1/N​.
qc-w1d4: A circuit is a recipe read left to right: qubits start in ∣0⟩|0\rangle∣0⟩, gates change them, and measurements give bitstrings that Qiskit writes with qubit 0 on the right.
qc-w1d5: A qubit is a pair of complex amplitudes; measuring it gives random bits with probabilities ∣amplitude∣2|\text{amplitude}|^2∣amplitude∣2; gates like RY(θ)R_Y(\theta)RY​(θ) set those odds; and only many shots, with honest error bars, tell you what the state was.
qc-w2d1: A qubit state is a point on the Bloch sphere: latitude θ\thetaθ sets the measurement odds, longitude φ\varphiφ is a phase that a 0/1 measurement can't see but gates can use.
qc-w2d2: The Pauli gates are half-turns of the Bloch sphere: X flips the bit, Z flips the phase, Y does both. Each undoes itself, and each leaves the two states on its own axis alone.
qc-w2d3: H turns ∣0⟩,∣1⟩|0\rangle, |1\rangle∣0⟩,∣1⟩ into ∣+⟩,∣−⟩|+\rangle, |-\rangle∣+⟩,∣−⟩ and back; it swaps the z and x views of the qubit; and two H's cancel, because amplitudes can interfere.
qc-w2d4: Every one-qubit gate is a rotation of the Bloch sphere: X, Y, Z are half turns about the axes, H swaps the x and z axes, S and T are small turns about z, and RX, RY, RZ turn by any angle you choose.
qc-w2d5: Every one-qubit state is a point on the Bloch sphere and every one-qubit gate is a turn of it: Paulis are half-turns, H swaps the z and x views, phase gates and rotations turn by any angle, and two rotations can reach any point.
qc-w3d1: States are column vectors, gates are matrices whose columns say where ∣0⟩|0\rangle∣0⟩ and ∣1⟩|1\rangle∣1⟩ go, and a circuit is one product of matrices, read right to left.
qc-w3d2: Gates are unitary matrices (U†U=IU^\dagger U = IU†U=I): they keep total probability at 1, they're always reversible with U†U^\daggerU†, and a circuit is undone in reverse order; only measurement destroys information.
qc-w3d3: Add the amplitudes of every path to an outcome before squaring: paths in phase reinforce, paths out of phase cancel, and a phase shift turns that dial smoothly.
qc-w3d4: To measure in another basis, turn the state first: H for X, S† then H for Y. Each basis reads one coordinate of the Bloch arrow, P=(1+coordinate)/2P = (1 + \text{coordinate})/2P=(1+coordinate)/2.
qc-w3d5: States are vectors and gates unitary matrices, so every gate can be undone; amplitudes add and cancel (interference); a basis change before the meter reads the arrow along any axis, and three bases reveal the whole state.
qc-w4d1: nnn qubits carry 2n2^n2n amplitudes; independent qubits combine by the tensor product, where probabilities multiply; and Qiskit reads bitstrings right to left, with qubit 0 last.
qc-w4d2: CNOT flips a target when its control is 1; after an H it creates a Bell state whose outcomes always agree, a state that can't be split into two separate qubits: that is entanglement.
qc-w4d3: The four Bell states are perfectly correlated in every basis while each qubit alone is pure randomness; their correlation signs identify them, and the CHSH test shows no pre-arranged trick can mimic them.
qc-w4d4: GHZ states tie many qubits into one decision; writing a general nnn-qubit state takes 2n2^n2n amplitudes, so every qubit doubles a simulation's cost, a wall that entanglement builds and quantum computers simply climb.
qc-w4d5: An expectation value is the average of an observable's ±1 outcomes; ⟨X⟩\langle X\rangle⟨X⟩, ⟨Y⟩\langle Y\rangle⟨Y⟩, ⟨Z⟩\langle Z\rangle⟨Z⟩ are the Bloch arrow's coordinates, ZZZZZZ measures correlation, and on hardware every one of them is estimated from shots.
qc-w5d1: Teleportation sends an unknown qubit using a shared Bell pair, a CNOT and an H, two measured bits sent by ordinary means, and a Pauli fix; it never copies the state and never beats light.
qc-w5d2: With a shared Bell pair, Alice encodes two bits by applying I, X, Z or ZX to her half, sends that one qubit, and Bob reads both bits with a CNOT and an H; the traveling qubit alone reveals nothing.
qc-w5d3: An oracle computes fff reversibly; with its output qubit in ∣−⟩|-\rangle∣−⟩ the answers kick back as signs (−1)f(x)(-1)^{f(x)}(−1)f(x), and Hadamards before and after make those signs interfere, so a single query tells constant from balanced.
qc-w5d4: For f(x)=s⋅x mod 2f(x) = s \cdot x \bmod 2f(x)=s⋅xmod2, Deutsch–Jozsa's circuit returns the secret sss in one query, because kickback flips exactly the qubits where sss has a 1 and the final Hadamards turn those flips into 1s.
qc-w5d5: Entanglement carries qubits and bits (teleportation, superdense coding), phase kickback turns answers into signs, and interference turns signs into results: one query for Deutsch–Jozsa and Bernstein–Vazirani, and about π4N\frac{\pi}{4}\sqrt{N}4π​N​ for Grover's search.
qc-w6d1: Noise turns pure states into mixed ones, shrinking the Bloch arrow into the ball: depolarizing evenly, dephasing sideways, amplitude damping towards ∣0⟩|0\rangle∣0⟩; on hardware it grows with time (T1T_1T1​, T2T_2T2​) and with every gate.
qc-w6d2: A density matrix ρ=∑kpk∣ψk⟩⟨ψk∣\rho = \sum_k p_k|\psi_k\rangle\langle\psi_k|ρ=∑k​pk​∣ψk​⟩⟨ψk​∣ is the complete description of a quantum state: probabilities on the diagonal, phases off it, purity between ½ and 1 for a qubit; different recipes can give the same ρ\rhoρ, and the parts of an entangled pair are mixed.
qc-w6d3: Fidelity (1 = same) and trace distance (0 = same, half the tip-to-tip distance for a qubit) measure closeness; the Helstrom bound says one measurement identifies one of two equally likely states with probability at most ½(1 + D), reached by measuring along their difference.
qc-w6d4: A chip offers few native gates and limited connectivity, so the transpiler translates gates, chooses a layout, routes with SWAPs (three CNOTs each) and optimizes; every CNOT it adds is extra noise, so layout and chip-aware circuit design matter.
qc-w6d5: Noise shrinks Bloch arrows into the ball (mixed states, described by density matrices), fidelity and trace distance measure the damage and bound how well states can be told apart, transpiling to a real chip adds CNOTs and noise, and mitigation (calibration and zero-noise extrapolation) recovers good averages at the price of extra shots.
qc-w7d1: Parameterized circuits leave gate angles open; an ansatz repeats rotation and entangling layers with n(L+1)n(L + 1)n(L+1) knobs; and its expressibility, which states its knobs can reach, depends on its gates: without entangling gates, no entanglement.
qc-w7d2: A cost such as ⟨H⟩\langle H\rangle⟨H⟩ turns knob settings into a landscape; every one-knob slice is a sine wave fixed by three evaluations; landscapes have local minima that trap small steps; and shot noise blurs the map.
qc-w7d3: Because each knob's cost is a sine wave, half the difference between runs shifted by ±π2\pm\frac\pi2±2π​ is the exact slope; it tolerates shot noise far better than small-step finite differences, at a cost of two circuits per knob.
qc-w7d4: VQE minimizes a measured energy ⟨H⟩\langle H\rangle⟨H⟩ over a circuit's knobs, with parameter-shift gradients and a classical optimizer; the variational principle makes every result an upper bound on the ground-state energy, and an entangling ansatz reaches chemical accuracy for H₂.
qc-w7d5: Parameterized circuits are trainable models: their landscapes are sine waves along every knob, their slopes come exactly from the parameter-shift rule, they can solve real problems like H₂ with VQE, and their big, deep versions risk barren plateaus that call for local costs, shallow structure and careful starts.
qml-w1d1: QML sorts into CC, CQ, QC and QQ; a quantum model encodes, processes, measures and learns; and for ordinary data, every claim must beat a strong classical baseline.
qml-w1d2: Basis encoding turns bits into basis states, angle encoding turns each scaled feature into a rotation of its own qubit (or two features per qubit with dense encoding), and the scale decides whether data points stay distinguishable.
qml-w1d3: Amplitude encoding stores 2n2^n2n normalized numbers in nnn qubits, but generally costs about 2n2^n2n gates to prepare and many shots to read, so practical QML usually shrinks the data with PCA and angle-encodes what's left.
qml-w1d4: Entangling feature maps such as the ZZ map make the encoded state depend on products of features, which twists the similarity landscape; that can help or just add wiggles, so feature maps are chosen on held-out data, like any kernel.
qml-w1d5: The swap test turns the fidelity of any two states into the ancilla's probability (1+F)/2(1 + F)/2(1+F)/2; the inversion test reads it directly as P(00…0)P(00\ldots0)P(00…0) when the circuits are known; both cost shots, for every pair of points.
qml-w2d1: A quantum kernel encodes data into quantum states and uses their fidelity as the similarity for a classical SVM; whether it helps depends on the feature map, and a badly scaled encoding makes every point look alike or every point look different.
qml-w2d2: A quantum-kernel SVM needs N(N−1)2\frac{N(N-1)}{2}2N(N−1)​ training circuits and M×NM \times NM×N test circuits, each a shot estimate; shot noise turns the zero eigenvalues of the kernel matrix negative, and clipping them restores a valid kernel.
qml-w2d3: A quantum SVM is an SVM with a quantum kernel: shrink and scale on the training set, cross-validate the bandwidth and CCC with precomputed kernels, test once, and compare with an equally tuned classical kernel.
qml-w2d4: As qubits are added, expressive quantum kernels concentrate: different points get values near 2−n2^{-n}2−n that shots can't resolve, so the model memorizes; a small bandwidth restores the spread, but may leave little that's truly quantum.
qml-w2d5: A quantum kernel is a similarity measured by a circuit and handed to an ordinary SVM: tune its bandwidth, watch for concentration, compare it with a tuned classical kernel over many splits, and on small classical datasets expect a tie.
qml-w3d1: A variational quantum classifier uploads the data as angles, processes it with trainable rotations and entanglement, predicts from the sign of ⟨Z⟩\langle Z\rangle⟨Z⟩, and trains by gradient descent with parameter-shift gradients, at N(1+2P)N(1 + 2P)N(1+2P) circuit runs per epoch.
qml-w3d2: Measurement counts estimate the Born-rule probability (1−⟨Z⟩)/2(1 - \langle Z\rangle)/2(1−⟨Z⟩)/2, which cross-entropy can train and a classical scale can sharpen; two qubits give four class probabilities for free; and shots blur only the points within about 1/S1/\sqrt{S}1/S​ of the boundary.
qml-w3d3: Give a circuit a backward pass made of parameter-shift runs, for its weights and its input angles, and PyTorch trains it inside any hybrid model; then use a classical twin and a frozen encoder to check whether the circuit is doing the work.
qml-w3d4: A circuit that uploads xxx through rotation gates is a Fourier series in xxx: LLL uploads give frequencies up to LLL, trainable gates only set their amounts, and re-uploading, one after another or in parallel, is what makes a quantum model expressive.
qml-w3d5: A variational quantum classifier encodes, processes and measures, turns counts into probabilities, trains like any PyTorch layer, and gets its expressiveness from re-uploading; on small classical datasets it ties a network of the same size, at a far higher price.
qml-w4d1: Gate noise shrinks a classifier's scores, relaxation and readout errors shift them, and deep noisy circuits lose their gradients exponentially: re-tune on the device to undo shifts, spend shots to fight shrinking, and keep circuits shallow.
qml-w4d2: The circuits we can train tend to be the circuits classical computers can imitate: a re-uploading classifier is exactly a linear model on its Fourier features, so every quantum claim needs a strong classical baseline, a surrogate check, and evidence of where classical imitation stops scaling.
qml-w4d3: When the data are quantum states, the measurement is part of the model: the Helstrom bound caps every learner at 12(1+D)\frac{1}{2}(1 + D)21​(1+D), a trainable measurement can reach it, measuring in the wrong basis first can erase the answer, and the clearest quantum advantages in learning come from data like these.
qml-w4d4: Read a QML paper for its claim, check the claim against the evidence (protocol, baselines, selection, shots and noise, scale, simulability, cost and the data's origin), and when you can, reproduce it small: the ad hoc dataset shows a real but narrow effect, a matched kernel learning from few examples.
qml-w4d5: A mini-study is a question, a hypothesis written first, a fair protocol, numbers with their spread and an honest verdict with its limits, and with three tutorials behind you, you can run one from the classical baseline to the quantum circuit.
